title: Shifting Power and the Causes of World War I
subject: AP World History

chunks.text: Around 1900 the global balance of power was shifting rapidly. Older land-based and Islamic empires were weakening or collapsing while newly industrialized nation-states rose, jostling for dominance in an increasingly dangerous international order.

The Ottoman Empire, once a superpower spanning three continents, had declined so badly that Europeans called it the 'sick man of Europe.' It was losing territory in the Balkans and North Africa and survived partly because the great powers could not agree on how to divide it.

Qing China, humiliated by the Opium Wars, the unequal treaties, and the Boxer Rebellion, continued to weaken and collapsed entirely in 1911, ending more than two thousand years of imperial dynastic rule in China.

Russia was an enormous but autocratic and only partly industrialized empire. It was shaken by a revolution in 1905 and humiliated by its defeat in the Russo-Japanese War of 1904–1905, exposing its relative weakness among the great powers.

Germany, unified only in 1871, industrialized with astonishing speed and by 1900 had surpassed Britain in steel and chemical production. As a young, ambitious power it demanded colonies, naval strength, and recognition as a world leader, unsettling the established powers, especially Britain.

The United States became an industrial giant and, after the Spanish-American War of 1898, an overseas imperial power. Japan, modernized through the Meiji Restoration, defeated Russia in 1905 — the first modern victory of an Asian power over a European great power — electrifying anti-colonial movements.

The Balkans were called 'the powder keg of Europe': a region of small, newly independent, fiercely nationalist states wedged between the collapsing Ottoman Empire and the multi-ethnic Austro-Hungarian Empire. It was the most dangerous flashpoint in Europe.

Historians organize the long-term causes of World War I with the acronym M.A.I.N.: Militarism, Alliances, Imperialism, and Nationalism. None alone caused the war; together, over decades, they turned Europe into a powder keg ready to explode.

Militarism was the glorification of military power and the belief that a strong, ready military was the key to national greatness. Great powers built ever-larger armies and navies, drew up detailed war plans, and treated war as a legitimate instrument of policy.

The naval arms race between Britain and Germany was the clearest example of militarism. After Germany began building modern dreadnought battleships to challenge British naval supremacy, the two powers competed to out-build each other, deepening hostility.

Two alliance blocs divided Europe: the Triple Alliance of Germany, Austria-Hungary, and Italy, and the Triple Entente of France, Russia, and Britain. Meant to deter war by balancing power, the alliances could instead pull every member into a local conflict.

Imperial rivalry fueled tension as the great powers competed for colonies, markets, and prestige. Crises over Morocco repeatedly raised tensions, and Germany resented arriving late to the colonial scramble while Britain and France held vast empires.

Nationalism was the combustible emotional fuel of WWI, making citizens aggressive and eager to prove their nation's superiority. Most dangerously, Slavic nationalism in the Balkans — backed by Russia — demanded independence from the Austro-Hungarian Empire.

On June 28, 1914, Gavrilo Princip, a Bosnian Serb nationalist, assassinated Archduke Franz Ferdinand, heir to the Austro-Hungarian throne, and his wife Sophie in Sarajevo. This was the immediate trigger, or spark, of World War I.

The assassination of Franz Ferdinand was the immediate trigger of WWI, not its underlying cause. It led to a world war only because of the long-term M.A.I.N. pressures already in place. Distinguishing the spark from the gunpowder is a core causation skill.

In the July Crisis of 1914, Austria-Hungary blamed Serbia, received a 'blank check' of unconditional support from Germany, and issued Serbia a deliberately unacceptable ultimatum before declaring war on July 28, 1914.

After Austria-Hungary declared war on Serbia, the alliance system acted like dominoes: Russia mobilized to protect Serbia, Germany declared war on Russia and France, and Germany's invasion of neutral Belgium brought Britain into the war. Within a week all great powers were at war.

Germany's war plan, the Schlieffen Plan, called for quickly defeating France by attacking through neutral Belgium before turning to fight Russia. The violation of Belgian neutrality is what brought Britain into the war against Germany.

Japan's 1905 defeat of Russia symbolized the broader global shift in power: it was the first time in the modern era that an industrialized Asian power decisively beat a European great power, inspiring nationalists across Asia and Africa.

World War I eventually killed roughly seventeen million people and pulled in soldiers and colonies from Africa, Asia, the Pacific, and the Americas, making a crisis that began in the Balkans into a truly global conflict.

Strong causation analysis distinguishes the immediate trigger (the assassination) from underlying long-term causes (M.A.I.N.), explains how they interacted (the assassination activated the alliance system), and weighs which causes mattered most rather than listing them as equal.

World War I is called 'the seminal catastrophe of the twentieth century' because so much that followed — the collapse of four empires, the Russian Revolution, the harsh peace that helped produce Hitler, the redrawing of the Middle East, and the weakening of colonial empires — flowed from it.
